extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, PTAB judges/attorneys, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Federal Circuit standards and tests for patent eligibility (§101/Alice), anticipation/printed-publication, on-sale bar, obviousness (motivation to combine, analogous art, result-effective-variable), double-patenting, and written-description; focused on how courts evaluate claims and prior-art evidence. Useful for attorneys preparing litigations, PTAB petitions, or counseling clients on claim drafting and prosecution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim selection for eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may select one or more claims as 'representative' of a broader group of claims for purposes of evaluating patent eligibility (e.g., district court analyzed claim 9 and the Federal Circuit also treated claims 11 and 16 as representative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative-claim treatment permits resolving §101 issues without analyzing every claim, but the chosen representative must fairly represent the claim set; appellate courts will scrutinize whether the representative characterization improperly characterizes claims at an impermissibly high level of generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step One — directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the representative claim is directed to an abstract idea (e.g., 'receiving information, associating information with images, comparing the images, and presenting information based on that comparison').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that recite generalized steps of collecting, analyzing, and presenting information using nothing other than the conventional operations of generic computer components are typically directed to abstract ideas. How the court articulates the abstract idea (level of generality) can be outcome-determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step Two — inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim is directed to an abstract idea, determine whether the claim recites an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea into patent-eligible application — the abstract idea itself cannot supply the inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely state functional results (e.g., 'using the object itself as the trigger for leaving information to be collected in the future') or that describe conventional techniques do not supply an inventive concept. If the specification or prosecution history shows methods were known or described as prior art, that undercuts an inventive-concept argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/result-oriented claim language undermines eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims characterized by result-oriented, functional language that omit specific requirements as to how steps are performed are more likely to be found directed to an abstract idea and ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for specificity about how a claimed result is achieved; merely reciting high-level functions without technical detail or nonconventional implementation favors ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims drawn to a specific technical solution may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a specific device or method that improves the relevant technology (e.g., an improved POV camera with dual recording configuration and wireless streaming of a low-quality stream to a remote device) can be treated as directed to a technical solution rather than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid characterizing such claims at an unduly high level of generality; emphasize the claimed technical improvements and concrete configuration/limitations that solve a technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague added limitations do not rescue eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding limitations that are vague (e.g., 'extracting and matching interest points') but do not explain how the limitation is performed or how it improves technology typically do not affect the §101 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations must provide specificity (how determined/used) and technical substance; mere labels for operations without implementation detail are insufficient to make claims 'significantly more' than an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed-publication prior art standard — accessibility to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: A document is a printed publication if it was disseminated to the interested public and reasonably accessible (e.g., an operating manual obtainable upon purchase or by request, corroborated by testimony, invoices, and emails).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution to a few customers under confidentiality may defeat publication; conversely, records showing manuals were available via purchase or request can establish printed-publication status. Courts examine intent to disseminate and evidence of public accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction must follow claim language and specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms should not be given restrictive meanings (e.g., requiring 'positioned above and in vertical and lateral alignment') unless the claim language or specification supports such a restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will reverse constructions that import limitations unsupported by the intrinsic record; claim construction should reflect ordinary meaning unless patentee acted as lexicographer or disavowed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: §102(b)(2)(B) — 'publicly disclosed by the inventor' requires public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'publicly disclosed by the inventor' in §102(b)(2)(B) means the subject matter was made available to the public, and does not encompass every disclosure under §102(a) (e.g., not every 'on sale' disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language and legislative history support a narrower meaning focused on public availability; private sales between individuals that do not make the invention available to the public do not qualify for the exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar for process inventions (pre-AIA continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under settled pre-AIA precedent, sales of products made using a secret process can trigger the on-sale bar to patentability; the AIA reenacted 'on sale' against the backdrop of that body of law and did not abrogate the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing applicability of the on-sale bar, consider pre-AIA precedents (Helsinn guidance) and whether Congress intended to change the settled meaning; courts presume continuity unless clear evidence of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA on-sale invalidity elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre-AIA §102(b) an on-sale invalidity determination requires: (1) the subject of the offer embodies the claims; (2) the offer was 'in this country'; (3) the offer occurred before the critical date; (4) the offer was a commercial offer for sale; and (5) the invention was ready for patenting prior to the critical date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply general contract principles to determine whether communications (e.g., a quotation letter) constitute a commercial offer; detailed, signed, and directed offers to a specific company can qualify even if no sale occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes an offer 'made in this country'
rubrics_metrics.description: An offer directed to a United States entity at its United States place of business is an offer 'made in this country' for purposes of the pre-AIA on-sale bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the geographic target and recipient of the offer; an offer aimed at a US company's US business location satisfies the statutory in-country requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: §102(b)(2)(B) application — private sale facts matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A private sale arranged via private messages between individuals, with no indication the inventor made the inventive subject matter available to the public, will not satisfy the 'publicly disclosed' exception and therefore the later publication can be prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine record evidence (who had access, publicity, fulfillment, corroborating documents) to decide whether a sale amounted to public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine / analogous art for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish obviousness, a POSA must have been motivated to combine the prior art references with a reasonable expectation of success; patent challengers typically present expert testimony and reference disclosures to show motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that two references address similar problems or complementary improvements can show motivation to combine; the court will examine whether a POSA would recognize advantages from combining the teachings (e.g., applying Li's shorter symbol periods to Talukdar's newer system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art need not explicitly state a benefit if a POSA would recognize it
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference need not explicate why a teaching is beneficial so long as a person of ordinary skill in the art would recognize that the application of the teaching would be beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts accept implicit teachings that a POSA would appreciate; expert testimony explaining why a POSA would be motivated can be persuasive absent contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-effective-variable and routine optimization analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'result-effective variable' doctrine is part of routine optimization analysis: an undisclosed parameter (e.g., molecular weight range) may be considered a result-effective variable that a POSA would optimize, and overlap in disclosed ranges is not strictly required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will consider whether parameters are typical/expected (supported by other prior-art data or expert testimony) and whether routine optimization would have led to the claimed value with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation-to-combine requires more than known alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere recognition that multiple arrangements or alternative systems existed in the prior art is insufficient; a proper motivation to combine requires articulation of reasons, advantages, or a substitution rationale a skilled artisan would have had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjectural or conclusory expert testimony that offers no rationale for substitution is inadequate; petitions and declarations should explain why a POSA would replace one arrangement with another and what problem the combination solves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard — reasonable expectation of success suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of obviousness does not require a guarantee of success; it requires that a POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of success in bridging gaps in the prior art to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that prior art provided specific reasons a POSA would be motivated and would have expected success; absence of 'only failures' in the prior art supports a reasonable-expectation finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description possession requirement and interpretation of 'optional'
rubrics_metrics.description: For §112 written-description, the specification must show that the inventors possessed the claimed invention. Use of the term 'optional' in the specification indicates something may be present or absent; embodiments and originally filed claims are part of the specification for this analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will look for explicit disclosure or embodiments supporting absence/inclusion of elements. Expert testimony about POSITA practices may be weighed, but objective specification disclosures and original claim content are critical. Minority/dissenting views may give weight to unrebutted expert testimony but majority decisions will rely on textual disclosures and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate standard — substantial evidence review of PTAB fact findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit review of PTAB factual findings (e.g., motivation to combine, whether a reference teaches a beneficial use) is governed by the substantial evidence standard; conclusions unsupported by substantial evidence will be reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigants should ensure the administrative record contains adequate evidentiary support (expert analysis, citations to specific disclosures) because conclusory assertions are unlikely to survive appellate review.
